LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman dates a much older man, bystanders often speculate that she has only the most superficial of motives. French actress Ludivine Sagnier stars in veteran New Wave filmmaker Claude Chabrol's "The Girl Cut in Two." In "The Girl Cut in Two," veteran French filmmaker Claude Chabrol tells the story of one young woman for whom just the opposite is true. It stars French starlet Ludivine Sagnier as a young woman who rejects the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy man her age, in favor of a sleazy affair with a fickle, 60 year-old father figure. Sagnier's desire to take on the role was also motivated by the allure of a much older man: Chabrol. "The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave." "The guy has so much experience. I felt like I was a journalist, always asking things," continues Sagnier. "He's very old ... he's been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that." Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige, a charming, 20-something television weather girl, as "very naive." "She falls in a trap like a poor little lamb and she gets eaten by wolves. "The thing is, she doesn't have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes. "I'd say I'm stronger than that," says 29 year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best-known for her provocative portrayal of a highly-sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in Francois Ozon's 2003 drama, "Swimming Pool." Sagnier who is often compared with screen sirens like Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, drew international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003, but has recently has been taking smaller roles. Many of the qualities that attracted Sagnier to Chabrol are similar to those that draw her on-screen alter-ego Gabrielle to writer Charles Saint-Denis (Francois Berleand) -- Charles' knowledge of life, literature and his ability to treat her like a little girl, not as an equal. Sagnier says of working with Chabrol: "It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. "He met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes, so you want to know more." Chabrol began his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and Francois Truffaut. He became famous in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidele" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971). He has continued working prolifically in film and television ever since. Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for the heartbreak drama, in which Sagnier character is consistently disappointed in love and let down by the men around her, with his step-daughter, Cecile Maistre, who also served as assistant director on the film. At the end of "The Girl Cut In Two," Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling in the spotlight as she hears applause rise from the audience, the attention perhaps curing her depression over lovers lost. She lies in a box, appearing to be cut in half, the trick functioning as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title -- but clearly there's more to it than meets the eye. "She cuts into two men first of all, and she's also cut in two different sides of her personality," said Sagnier. "She has a part of shade and a part of lightness." Sagnier's fate since her collaboration with Chabrol has, thankfully, been a decidedly rosier affair: Since finishing "The Girl Cut in Two," she has starred in Jean-Francois Richet's, "Public Enemy No. 1," which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 Cesar Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars. The indefatigable Chabrol has recently wrapped up yet another film: "Bellamy" starring Gerard Depardieu. "The Girl Cut In Two" is released in the UK on 22 May 2009 .

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — When a young woman dates a significantly older man, public perception often assumes superficial motives. However, in *The Girl Cut in Two*, veteran French New Wave director Claude Chabrol presents a compelling subversion of this cliché. Starring French actress Ludivine Sagnier, the film centers on a young woman who rejects the amorous advances of a wealthy, flashy peer in favor of a sordid affair with a fickle, 60-year-old father figure.

Off-screen, Sagnier’s interest in the project was similarly driven by the appeal of an older man: Chabrol himself. "The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave." 

Reflecting on his expansive career, Sagnier added: "The guy has so much experience. I felt like I was a journalist, always asking things... He's very old ... he's been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that."

Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige—a charming television weather presenter in her twenties—as "very naive." 

"She falls in a trap like a poor little lamb and she gets eaten by wolves," Sagnier observed. "The thing is, she doesn't have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes." 

"I'd say I'm stronger than that," noted the 29-year-old actress, who is perhaps best known for her provocative portrayal of a highly sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in François Ozon's 2003 drama *Swimming Pool*. Frequently compared to screen icons like Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, Sagnier earned international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003, though she has taken on smaller roles in recent years.

Intriguingly, the qualities that drew Sagnier to Chabrol mirror those that attract her on-screen alter ego, Gabrielle, to the writer Charles Saint-Denis (played by François Berléand)—namely, his sophisticated knowledge of life and literature, alongside his tendency to treat her as a child rather than an equal. 

Speaking about her time working with the auteur, Sagnier recalled: "It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. He met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes, so you want to know more."

Chabrol launched his career in 1956, establishing his reputation alongside fellow New Wave luminaries Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. He achieved widespread acclaim in the late 1960s with acclaimed suspense thrillers such as *La Femme Infidèle* (1969) and *Le Boucher* (1971), and he has maintained a remarkably prolific career in film and television ever since. 

For *The Girl Cut in Two*—a heartbreak drama in which Sagnier's character is consistently let down by the men in her life—Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay with his stepdaughter, Cécile Maistre, who also served as the film's assistant director.

In the film's conclusion, Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling beneath the spotlight as applause rises from the audience—a moment of public acclaim that perhaps offers solace for her lost loves. As she lies in a box, seemingly sawed in half, the illusion serves as a literal embodiment of the film's title, though Sagnier notes a deeper psychological layer to the scene.

"She cuts into two men first of all, and she's also cut in two different sides of her personality," Sagnier explained. "She has a part of shade and a part of lightness."

Fortunately, Sagnier’s own trajectory since collaborating with Chabrol has been a decidedly brighter affair. Since wrapping *The Girl Cut in Two*, she starred in Jean-François Richet’s *Public Enemy No. 1*, which earned more nominations than any other film at the 2009 César Awards—France’s equivalent of the Oscars. Meanwhile, the indefatigable Chabrol recently completed yet another feature, *Bellamy*, starring Gérard Depardieu. 

*The Girl Cut in Two* opens in UK cinemas on May 22, 2009.

# Ludivine Sagnier shines in Claude Chabrol’s deliciously dark 'The Girl Cut in Two'

**By CNN Entertainment Staff** 

**(CNN) —** In French auteur Claude Chabrol’s cinematic mind game, *The Girl Cut in Two*, the title isn’t just a reference to a magician’s illusion—it’s a biting metaphor for a woman torn apart by the vanity, power, and dark desires of the men around her. 

Standing squarely at the center of this psychological storm is Ludivine Sagnier, delivering a magnetic performance that proves she is far more than just French cinema’s favorite siren. 

In *The Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*), Sagnier plays Gabrielle Deneige, a bubbly television weather presenter in Lyon whose infectious charm captures the attention of two radically different—and equally dangerous—suitors. 

First comes Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand), a brilliant, married, and deeply cynical literary icon who introduces Gabrielle to a world of perverted intellectual games. Then comes Paul Gaudens (Benoît Magimel), a spoiled, wildly unhinged heir to a pharmaceutical empire who views Gabrielle not just as a lover, but as a prize to be won at any cost. 

What ensues is a icy, slow-burn tragedy of obsession, vanity, and bourgeois hypocrisy. 

### From Muse to Leading Lady

Sagnier, who first captivated international audiences with her sultry, breakthrough turns in François Ozon’s *8 Women* (2002) and *Swimming Pool* (2003), elevates Chabrol’s wicked thriller with a performance of subtle heartbreak. 

Instead of playing Gabrielle as a passive damsel in distress, Sagnier imbues her with a tragic innocence. She is a woman who simply wants to be loved, yet finds herself objectified by two men who view her as an extension of their own fragile egos. 

"Sagnier brings a fascinating vulnerability to the role," noted CNN film critics during the festival circuit. "She allows Gabrielle to be naive without ever making her foolish, making her inevitable unraveling all the more painful to watch."

### The "French Hitchcock" Strikes Again

For Chabrol, often dubbed the "French Hitchcock," the film is a return to his favorite sandbox: dissecting the cruelties of the French upper class. At 77 years old, the veteran French New Wave director shows zero interest in softening his edge. 

With a cool, almost clinical detachment, Chabrol masterfully shifts the tone of the film from a breezy romantic comedy to a suffocating revenge drama. 

True crime aficionados will recognize the real-life inspiration behind the plot: the infamous 1906 murder of legendary architect Stanford White by millionaire Harry Kendall Thaw over Gilded Age showgirl Evelyn Nesbit. Chabrol takes that historic American scandal and transplants it seamlessly into modern-day French high society, complete with sleek television studios, cozy bookshops, and oppressive country estates.

### A Cut Above

The film culminates in a literal illusion—a magician's stage trick involving a box and a saw—that doubles as a searing commentary on how media, money, and men consume young women. 

Supported by razor-sharp performances from Berléand and Magimel, *The Girl Cut in Two* is a sleek, darkly funny, and ultimately sobering entry in Chabrol’s massive filmography. 

In the hands of a lesser actress, Gabrielle might have been reduced to a simple plot device—the prize in a game of toxic masculinity. But under Chabrol’s sharp lens and anchored by Sagnier’s star-making work, *The Girl Cut in Two* ensures that even when the men try to slice her world in half, it is Sagnier who commands every inch of the screen.

*‘The Girl Cut in Two’ is currently playing in select theaters and available on VOD.*

In "The Girl Cut in Two" (*La Fille coupée en deux*), Sagnier takes center stage in a dark, sophisticated satire that dissects the corrupting nature of passion, power, and the French bourgeoisie.

### A classic French triangle

In the film, Sagnier plays Gabrielle Deneige, a bright and deceptively innocent TV weather presenter in Lyon. Gabrielle finds herself emotionally fractured—quite literally "cut in two"—between two radically different suitors. 

On one side is Paul Gaudens (Benoît Magimel), a brilliant but wildly unpredictable young heir to a pharmaceutical fortune. On the other is Charles Saint-Denis (Charles Berling), a suave, world-weary novelist who is decades her senior.

"Gabrielle is a woman caught between two visions of love," Sagnier told CNN. "One represents the chaotic, reckless energy of youth, while the other offers intellect, sophistication, and worldliness. But both men ultimately want to possess her rather than understand her."

The narrative, loosely inspired by the infamous 1906 murder of American architect Stanford White by millionaire Harry Kendall Thaw over model Evelyn Nesbit, is transposed by Chabrol into modern-day France with characteristic sharp wit.

### Decoding the age gap

Central to the film’s tension is Gabrielle’s affair with the older writer, a dynamic that Sagnier believes is often misunderstood by audiences looking for simple moral answers.

"In modern society, we are still fascinated and scandalized by relationships with a significant age gap," Sagnier said. "When a young woman falls for an older man, people immediately assume it is about money or a search for a father figure. But for Gabrielle, it’s about mind over age. She is seduced by his intellect, his history, and his authority."

However, Sagnier is quick to point out the inherent power imbalance that Chabrol so meticulously exposes. 

"There is a vanity in older men who pursue younger women," she added. "They want to drink that youth to feel immortal again. It looks like mentorship or romance, but it can be profoundly selfish. Chabrol captures that ambiguity so brilliantly—he doesn’t judge the characters, but he exposes their flaws."

### Working with a New Wave pioneer

For Sagnier, who first shot to international fame in François Ozon’s "Swimming Pool" (2003), working with Chabrol was a milestone. 

Now 78, Chabrol is widely celebrated as one of the founding fathers of the *Nouvelle Vague* (French New Wave), the groundbreaking film movement of the late 1950s and 1960s that revolutionized global cinema alongside contemporaries like François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard. "To work with Claude is to step into living cinema history," Sagnier said. "You expect a dictator, a heavy patriarch of the French New Wave, but instead, you get a warm, mischievous grandfather who cares as much about what everyone is having for lunch as he does about the camera setup."

Sagnier noted that Chabrol’s light touch on set belies the dark precision of his storytelling. "He directs with incredible ease. He doesn't over-explain. He trusts his actors, but his eye is so sharp—he sees every tiny lie your character tells."

### Bringing a dark satire to the UK

"The Girl Cut in Two" has already drawn praise on the festival circuit for its sleek visuals and biting irony, cementing Sagnier's reputation as one of France's most versatile leading ladies. 

As the film prepares to hit British cinemas, Sagnier hopes audiences will appreciate the story's wicked sense of humor beneath its tragic exterior.

"It is a warning about idealizing love," Sagnier said. "Whether it is the illusion of a grand romantic mentor or the fantasy of a passionate young prince, reality usually cuts you down the middle."

**CNN Entertainment** — 

In the late, formidable stretch of his career, the master of French cinema Claude Chabrol possessed an uncanny ability to peel back the polished veneer of the French bourgeoisie to reveal the predatory instinct beneath. Nowhere is this surgical precision more apparent than in his 2007 dark satire, *The Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*). 

At the center of Chabrol’s modern reinterpretation of a notorious 20th-century scandal is Ludivine Sagnier, playing Gabrielle Deneige—a luminous, ambitious TV weather presenter who finds herself psychologically and emotionally bisected by two very different men. 

Speaking about the film’s enduring examination of power, age, and obsession, Sagnier reflects on a role that challenged the traditional cinematic tropes of the ingenue.

“When you read a Chabrol script, you realize nothing is accidental,” Sagnier tells CNN. “Gabrielle is not just caught in a love triangle. She is caught between two distinct generations of male ego, both using desire as a language of control.”

### The Poisoned Chalice of Mentorship

The catalyst for the film’s tragicomedy is Gabrielle’s obsession with Charles Saint-Denis (played with suave cynicism by François Berléand), a celebrated, middle-aged novelist who resides in a world of literary salons and quiet decadent luxury. For Gabrielle, Charles represents the ultimate archetype of the cultured mentor—a older man who offers her entry into a world far removed from her mundane studio life.

However, as Sagnier notes, the boundary between mentorship and manipulation quickly blurs under Chabrol’s lens. 

“When you are young and impressionable, wisdom can easily be mistaken for love,” Sagnier says. “Gabrielle looks at Charles and sees a guide, someone who will elevate her. But Charles’ idea of mentorship is inherently corrupting. He doesn’t want to help her grow; he wants to curate her innocence, to teach her his own brand of dark, perverted desire while keeping his quiet domestic life entirely intact.”

The dynamic highlights a reoccurring theme in Chabrol’s filmography: the predatory nature of the elder intelligentsia. Charles’ age gives him a tactical advantage over Gabrielle. He weaponizes his experience, using philosophical discourse and paternal warmth to lure her into a master-slave dynamic disguised as liberation. 

“It is a very subtle form of power,” Sagnier observes. “Charles tells her he is setting her free sexually, but really, he is binding her to his rules. Age, in this film, brings not wisdom, but a sophisticated cruelty.”

### The Anatomy of Desire: Possession vs. Passion

If Charles represents the calculated, patriarchal side of desire, Gabrielle’s second suitor—Paul Gaudens (Benoît Magimel), a volatile, unhinged heir to a pharmaceutical fortune—represents its raw, juvenile madness. Paul’s attraction to Gabrielle is frantic and consumeristic; he does not want to mentor her; he simply wants to own her.

This push-and-pull leaves Gabrielle split down the middle—drawn to the intellect of an older man who will never fully commit to her, and pursued by a younger man whose manic devotion borders on dangerous possession.

“Desire in Chabrol’s world is rarely clean,” Sagnier explains. “It’s a transaction. With Paul, it’s about youth reacting against youth—his desire is violent because he feels entitled to her. With Charles, it’s about legacy and vanity. Gabrielle is caught in the crossfire because she genuinely craves affection, but she is handed currency instead.”

Sagnier’s performance brilliantly captures the tragic irony at the heart of the film: Gabrielle believes she is the orchestrator of her own sexual awakening, only to discover she is the rope in a tug-of-war between two men attempting to assert their dominance over one another.

### "Cut in Two": Autonomy in the Aftermath

The film’s title operates both literally and figuratively. As the narrative spirals toward its shocking, public climax, Gabrielle’s sense of self is fragmented by the choices forced upon her by her lovers.

Yet, Sagnier refuses to view Gabrielle simply as a victim of male ambition and age disparity. Instead, she credits Chabrol with offering a subtle critique of female resilience in a world constructed by men.

“By the end of the story, she has been emotionally torn apart—she is literally 'the girl cut in two,'” Sagnier says. “But Claude gave her a survival instinct. In the final scenes, when she participates in an actual stage illusion where she is sawn in half, it’s a brilliant meta-metaphor. She allows the world to see her as broken, but she walks away whole.”

Nearly two decades after its release, *The Girl Cut in Two* remains a startlingly contemporary text. In an era where conversations surrounding age gaps, power dynamics, and consent dominate public discourse, Chabrol’s film—and Sagnier’s nuanced portrayal—stands as a haunting portrait of what happens when youth and desire are swallowed whole by the appetites of powerful men.

“Gabrielle taught me a lot about the illusion of control,” Sagnier reflects. “In the end, the real trick isn’t surviving the saw—it’s learning how to put yourself back together.”

**The Art of Being Torn: Ludivine Sagnier on Claude Chabrol, Illusion, and Father Figures**

When Ludivine Sagnier stepped onto the set of Claude Chabrol’s *A Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*) in 2007, she was already celebrated as the shimmering *enfant terrible* of French cinema. Having spent her early twenties tantalizing audiences in François Ozon’s *Water Drops on Burning Rocks* and *Swimming Pool*, Sagnier possessed a sun-drenched, deceptive innocence. But it was Chabrol—the veteran grandmaster of the French New Wave, famed for his razor-sharp dissections of bourgeois hypocrisy—who looked past her blonde siren aesthetic and saw a tragic heroine capable of profound emotional ruin.

In the film, inspired by the real-life 1906 murder of architect Stanford White, Sagnier plays Gabrielle Deneige, a charming TV weather girl who finds herself literally and emotionally bisected by the attentions of two very different men: a unstable, wildly wealthy heir (Benoît Magimel) and a celebrated, much older novelist, Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand). 

It is Gabrielle’s obsession with Charles—a fickle, vanity-driven intellectual old enough to be her father—that drives the heart of the film. For Sagnier, exploring why a vibrant young woman would surrender her agency to an elderly, emotionally withholding man was the central psychological puzzle of the role.

### The Trappings of a Toxic Father Figure

"Gabrielle isn’t looking for a lover; she’s looking for a key to a world she thinks is grander than her own," Sagnier reflected during the film's promotion. The attraction to Charles is not merely physical; it is an alluring cocktail of intellectual validation and paternal shelter. 

Charles is charismatic, cultured, and speaks to Gabrielle as though she possesses a soul worth examining, a stark contrast to the superficial television world she inhabits. In him, she sees a father figure who can elevate her. Yet, Charles’s appeal lies precisely in his fickleness. He is a married man who offers just enough affection to keep her tethered, but retreats into bourgeois respectability whenever real commitment is required.

"When a young woman seeks approval from an older, powerful man, she often mistakes his cynicism for wisdom," Sagnier noted of her character’s plight. "Charles plays the benevolent mentor, but he is fundamentally selfish. He wants the brightness of her youth without any of the responsibility. The more he pushes her away, the more she hungers for his approval—because to lose him feels like losing her own worth."

Sagnier portrayed Gabrielle’s delusion with a heartbreaking delicate grace. She understood that Gabrielle was drawn to Charles’s paternal authority precisely because it felt safe, unaware that his emotional duplicity would leave her far more vulnerable than the open hostility of her younger, unhinged suitor. 

### The Master of Joy: Sagnier’s Admiration for Chabrol

Paradoxically, while Sagnier was playing a woman undone by a toxic male mentor on screen, her off-screen experience with Claude Chabrol was the exact opposite. For Sagnier, working with Chabrol was the fulfillment of a lifelong cinematic dream, and the director became a beloved, genuinely paternal figure in her real life.

"Claude was the ultimate benevolent patriarch of French cinema," Sagnier recalled with immense warmth. "On set, he was a genius who never took himself seriously. He dissected human cruelty in his movies, but in life, he was pure joy."

Chabrol, known for his love of good food, heavy lunches, and laughter, created an atmosphere that was notoriously cozy. For an actress diving into dark psychological territory, Chabrol’s legendary warmth was a sanctuary. 

"He had this extraordinary ability to direct you without ever imposing a heavy hand," Sagnier explained. "He didn't torture his actors to get a tragic performance. Instead, he made you feel completely safe, totally seen, and entirely trusted. You wanted to be brilliant just to hear his deep, booming laugh from behind the monitor."

Where the fictional Charles Saint-Denis used his intellect to manipulate and diminish Gabrielle, Chabrol used his formidable mastery of cinema to empower Sagnier. He allowed her to steer the film, treating her not as a passive muse, but as a full collaborator. 

### A Dual Legacy

*A Girl Cut in Two* remains one of the late Chabrol’s final masterpieces, and much of its enduring power rests on Sagnier’s shoulders. She captured the tragic irony of youth: the desperate desire to grow up too fast, and the fatal mistake of mistaking a man's age for his maturity.

Looking back on her time with Chabrol, who passed away in 2010, Sagnier views the film as a pivotal moment in her career—a masterclass in craft delivered by a man who showed her what true mentorship looked like. 

"In the movie, Gabrielle is broken by a man she looked up to," Sagnier reflected. "But in reality, being guided by Claude built me up. He showed me that you can make serious, devastating art while maintaining a generous, joyful heart. I will love him forever for that."

**LONDON, England (CNN)** -- Five years after captivating international audiences in François Ozon's sensual mystery *Swimming Pool*, French actress Ludivine Sagnier returns to British cinema screens in the dark, satirical thriller *The Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*), directed by legendary auteur Claude Chabrol.

Opening in UK theaters this Friday, the film stars Sagnier as Gabrielle Deneige, a charming TV weather presenter in Lyon who finds herself entangled in a toxic love triangle between an egoistic, married novelist twice her age (François Berléand) and an unhinged, heir to a pharmaceutical fortune (Benoît Magimel). Loosely based on the infamous 1906 American scandal involving Evelyn Nesbit, Stanford White, and Harry Kendall Thaw, the film is a classic Chabrolian critique of bourgeois hypocrisy, vanity, and obsession.

Speaking to CNN in London ahead of the release, Sagnier described working with Chabrol—often referred to as the "French Hitchcock"—as a career highlight. 

"Working with Claude was a total joy," Sagnier said. "He has this reputation for making dark, cynical movies about the rot beneath polite society, but on set, he is the warmest, happiest director you could ask for. He loves good food, he cracks jokes, and he trusts his actors entirely."

Sagnier noted that Chabrol allowed her to bring a crucial sense of agency to a character who might otherwise be viewed purely as a victim. 

"Claude didn’t want Gabrielle to be just a pawn between two powerful men," she explained. "He wanted her to have light, ambition, and a certain naivety that gets corrupted by their cruelty. He guided me with such subtlety."

The role represents another major milestone for the 28-year-old actress, whose career skyrocketed after her breakout turn opposite Charlotte Rampling in 2003's *Swimming Pool*. Her performance as the captivating, sun-drenched Julie turned her into an overnight international sensation—and instantly labeled her as French cinema's newest sex symbol. 

Reflecting on the whirlwind years following *Swimming Pool*, Sagnier admitted that navigating post-breakout fame required deliberate, sometimes difficult choices to avoid being typecast.

"After *Swimming Pool*, I was offered so many scripts where the requirement was essentially just to take my clothes off and look dangerous," Sagnier revealed. "It was flattering, but I knew that if I stayed in that box, my career would be very short. I had to fight to be seen as a versatile actress rather than just a blonde fantasy."

In the years since, Sagnier has consciously diversified her filmography, taking on period dramas like *A Secret*, musical comedies like *Love Songs* (*Les Chansons d'amour*), and even Hollywood projects like P.J. Hogan's *Peter Pan*, where she played Tinker Bell. 

"I wanted to work with directors who saw beyond the image," Sagnier said. "Taking time to do theater and choosing smaller, character-driven French films helped me find my footing again."

With *The Girl Cut in Two*, Sagnier combines her natural screen allure with a mature, dramatic depth, solidifying her status as one of European cinema's premier leading ladies. 

*The Girl Cut in Two* opens in select UK cinemas on Friday.
